messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: City Council Member
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Vignette:
Claire, a 39-year-old City Council Member, presents as articulate and composed, yet her posture is rigid, her hands tightly clasped in her lap. She has built a life of public service and order, a stark contrast to the chaos that defined her childhood. For decades, she believed she had successfully walled off the past, but in recent months, the walls have begun to crumble. The memories are from when she was nine years old, and they arrive not as a coherent story but as a series of jagged, sensory fragments. She remembers the high, thin shattering sound of the crystal vase her mother loved, followed by a thick silence that was somehow louder. She can see, with perfect, searing clarity, the dark floral pattern on her mother’s dress against the beige carpet. But the moments leading up to the fall, what was said, and what her father’s face looked like, are a complete blank. Trying to grasp these missing pieces, she says, feels like reaching into fog; there is simply nothing there.

These fractured images intrude at unpredictable moments. During a particularly contentious budget meeting last month, a man in the front row stood up and began shouting about tax levies. Instantly, without conscious thought, Claire felt her shoulders hunch and her body curl inward in her chair, a protective crouch she hadn't assumed in thirty years. It was the same position she had taken behind the armchair in her childhood living room, making herself as small as possible. The feeling was not one of memory, but of immediate, physical reenactment; her body knew the threat before her mind could process the man's words. She now understands that her work, once a source of pride, has become a minefield. She no longer hears the content of her constituents' concerns; instead, she obsessively scans their faces, their hands, their posture, searching for the subtle shift—the tightening jaw, the clenched fist—that she has come to believe is the universal prelude to eruption.

This constant threat monitoring has exhausted her. Sleep offers no respite. She lies awake for hours, her mind replaying every tense interaction from the day, listening to the house settle, her body wired for a danger that never comes. Her world has shrunk to the path between her home and her private office at City Hall. These are the only two places she feels a semblance of safety. Community barbecues, town hall meetings, and even grocery shopping have become impossible gauntlets of perceived threat. She has cancelled more public appearances in the last three months than in her entire previous term. Her chief of staff has gently pointed out that her declining visibility is becoming a political liability, but the thought of standing in an unpredictable crowd, of being unable to watch everyone at once, is paralyzing.

Her husband, Mark, has noticed her withdrawal, the way she flinches if he moves too quickly or raises his voice in frustration at the television. He doesn’t understand why she insists on locking the deadbolt the moment she comes home, or why she stopped going on their evening walks through the neighborhood. She has tried to explain, but the words feel inadequate. How can she tell him that she looks at every stranger and sees a potential for violence, that her own home only feels safe if it is a fortress? She came to therapy because she realized her life of carefully constructed safety had become a prison. She is terrified of losing the career she fought so hard to build, but even more so, she is terrified that the vigilance is the only thing keeping her safe, and that if she ever lets her guard down, the vase will shatter all over again.
